old: Rewrote a path before using it: a backslash became a slash, one leading "./" or "/" was dropped, and trailing slashes were dropped, so "a\\b", "./a" and "a/" were taken as "a/b", "a" and "a". A ".." or empty segment was kept as a literal name, and list("") listed every file.
new: Refuses a path that is absolute, contains a backslash or NUL, or has a ".", ".." or empty segment, with a RangeError and before the store is touched. That includes "a\\b", "./a", "a/", ".." and ""; list() with no folder lists every file.
why: One path names one file in every store. The file system store must refuse paths that could leave the workspace, and the memory store follows the same contract so a test can't pass on memory and fail on disk. See also contracts.definition-store and memory.definition-store.

old: put stored any string as the media type, including parameters ("text/plain; charset=utf-8") and line breaks.
new: put refuses a media type that isn't type/subtype of HTTP token characters, with a RangeError, and stores nothing. A malformed hash (upper case, wrong length, "../etc/passwd") gives null from get, as the old store already did for any unknown hash.
why: A media type ends up in HTTP headers and file metadata; a line break there could split a header. Parameters are left out so one blob has one plain type.

old: append(event) took one event and added it to its run, whatever its seq and whatever was stored before, so two writers could both append and a run could get gaps or repeated numbers.
new: append(runId, expectedSeq, events) adds the events only when the run's last stored seq is expectedSeq, and otherwise returns { ok: false, reason: "conflict", lastSeq } and stores nothing. Empty, misnumbered or other-run events are refused with a RangeError.
why: The run log is the source of truth for a run. Checking expectedSeq means two writers can never interleave events, and of two at the same seq exactly one wins.

old: Checked a value with plain Zod 4.6.7, which has no nesting limit: input nested deeper than the call stack allows threw a RangeError ("Maximum call stack size exceeded") instead of giving issues, and a value that contains itself was accepted.
new: parse first walks the input without recursion and, if it is nested more than 256 keys and indexes deep (MAX_DEPTH) or contains itself, returns one too_deep issue at the path of the first value past the limit, without running the schema. Up to 256 levels it gives the same verdict as plain Zod.
why: A file must never crash the check, and a value that contains itself is never a valid workspace file. Real workspace files are nowhere near 256 levels deep (the old guard schema nested 200 levels still passes), so no file that loaded before is refused now. It is the only schema-kit difference that remains on real Zod; see also schema-kit.old-schema-parity.

old: 784f78d packages/core/app/src/studio.ts:577-599: Studio.save() set pending to {} after writing, so a change made to a file while the save ran was lost.
new: Only the changes that were written are cleared. A file changed during the save stays unsaved with its new text. A failed write still leaves every change unsaved.
why: Losing an edit silently is data loss. Signed off by Liam (CTO) on HAL-117, comment eab55441; only a bug fix to users, so not for HAL-58.

area: app kernel: undo after a save
old: 784f78d packages/core/app/src/studio.ts:535-599: an undo step restored the older parsed workspace and unsaved map but left the saved files as they were, so the model and the files disagreed and nothing showed as unsaved.
new: Undoing past a save makes the file read its text from before the change and marks it unsaved. A saved new file comes back as an unsaved delete, a saved delete as the old file, unsaved. Redo is the mirror.
why: The model and the files must agree; this is how editors such as VS Code undo past a save. Signed off by Liam (CTO) on HAL-117, comment 0b30ec44.

area: app kernel: save twice, or with nothing to save
old: 784f78d packages/core/app/src/studio.ts:577-599: two saves at once both wrote every file and both finished; a save with nothing unsaved still ran and reported "Saved 0 files".
new: A save that starts while another runs waits, then writes only what is still unsaved. A save with nothing unsaved writes nothing and sends no events.
why: Writing every file twice, or reporting an empty save, is noise and a race. Signed off by Liam (CTO) on HAL-117, comment 0b30ec44.

old: 784f78d packages/core/schema/src/index.ts: the pattern /^[1-9]d*(m|h|d)$/ missed a backslash, so every interval of two or more digits failed with invalid_format at trigger.mail.every.
new: Any whole number from 1 followed by m, h or d passes. This is the known 15m bug the plan names (9.3 points 4 and 7.3).
why: The old pattern missed a backslash: the known 15m bug the approved plan names as an allowed difference (9.3 points 4 and 7.3). Signed off by Liam (CTO) on HAL-873, comment b803700b; not for HAL-58.

old: 784f78d: the loader checked the default deployment after loading, as an error between files with no line ("The default deployment ... is not listed"); the file's own schema passed.
new: The deployments file itself fails, with default-deployment-not-listed at default, line 1. The workspace still fails, as before.
why: The check needs only the deployments file, so it belongs to the file kind, where it gets a line. The workspace fails as before. Signed off by Liam (CTO) on HAL-873, comment b803700b; not for HAL-58.

old: 784f78d packages/core/config/src/workspace.ts parseSkillMarkdown: skill problems had a path and a code but no line or column.
new: The same path and code, with the line and column in the file (line 1 when there is no front matter).
why: Every problem in the new format has a line and a column, so an editor can always point at it. Same path and code as before. Signed off by Liam (CTO) on HAL-873, comment b803700b; not for HAL-58.

old: 784f78d parseSkillMarkdown: front matter that wasn't valid YAML was read as empty, so the skill failed for a missing name and description, with no line.
new: One YAML syntax problem, at the line where the YAML breaks (line 3 in the fixture). The file still fails.
why: The old loader hid the YAML error and blamed missing fields. The file still fails, now with the real cause and its line. Signed off by Liam (CTO) on HAL-873, comment b803700b; not for HAL-58.

old: An every trigger ran when now - lastRun was at least the interval, at the time of the check. With every: 30m and a last run at 09:45, the next run came at 10:15.
new: due gives the multiples of the interval counted from the Unix epoch in UTC that fall after the last tick, up to now. With every: 30m the runs are at :00 and :30 of every hour, whenever the last one ran. Slots are always in UTC, so long intervals land at fixed UTC times, not at the time the routine was saved: every: 1d runs at 00:00 UTC (01:00 or 02:00 in Amsterdam), and every: 7d runs on Thursdays, because 1970-01-01 was a Thursday. Intervals that don't divide a day, such as 5h, land at different hours each day. Anyone who wants a fixed local time should use schedule. nextRun gives the same slot, so the Studio shows the time the tick starts.
why: A slot that comes from the clock alone is the same on every tick and every host, so a repeated or late tick, or a second host, asks for the same run with the same run id and it starts once (routines.due-exactly-once). A time counted from the last run moves whenever a run starts late, and two hosts can disagree on it.

area: routines tick: a new every routine
old: An every routine that had never run started right away, on the first check after it was saved.
new: A new every routine waits for its first slot after the scheduler's last tick. With every: 1h, a routine saved at 10:20 first runs at 11:00.
why: due knows only the window since the last tick, not when each routine last ran, which keeps it the same on every host. Starting at once also meant every new or renamed every routine fired the moment it was saved, often while it was still being edited. A person who wants a run now can start it by hand.

old: A scheduled time counted as on time, for catchUp: none, while now was no more than 2 minutes after it.
new: The grace is 60 seconds (DEFAULT_TICK_POLICY.graceMs). A host can pass another value in its TickPolicy.
why: The old scheduler checked every 30 seconds, so 60 seconds still covers one late or lost check at that rate. With 2 minutes, a laptop waking from sleep could still start a catchUp: none run up to 2 minutes late, which that setting is meant to prevent.

old: catchUp: all returned at most the 20 newest missed times of a schedule; older ones were reported as skipped and dropped.
new: As in the old app, catchUp: all keeps the newest missed times and drops the older ones past the cap, but the cap is 100 instead of 20 (DEFAULT_TICK_POLICY.maxCatchUp). due returns at most the 100 newest missed times per routine, started oldest first. A host can pass another cap in its TickPolicy.
why: catchUp: all is for routines whose every run counts, such as hourly totals, so a weekend asleep (about 60 hourly times) should not lose any. 100 still bounds one tick. When the cap does cut, the newest times are the ones still worth running, and starting them oldest first lets the runs see their times in order.

area: routines tick: catchUp all in one tick
old: dueRoutines applied the routine's overlap setting in the same call, so with the default overlap: skip a catch-up started one run and reported the other missed times as skipped.
new: due returns every missed time a catchUp: all routine allows, up to the cap, in one tick. Whether they all start at once is up to the app's RoutineScheduler, which applies overlap (app.routine-overlap): allow starts them all, queue starts them one after another, skip starts one.
why: due can't know which runs are still going, so it can't apply overlap. Returning every allowed time keeps due a pure function of the window and lets the scheduler, which can ask the run store, decide.

old: dueRoutines returned, per routine, a skipped list: due times dropped by catchUp or because a run was still busy (overlap: skip).
new: due returns only the runs to start. Times that catchUp drops are left out without a list. Overlap is applied by the app's RoutineScheduler, which reports the times it skips because a run is busy (HAL-1007).
why: Nothing in the old app read the skipped list for catch-up; the old Studio only started what was in start. Keeping due a plain list of runs keeps it simple to check for exactly-once, and the skips a person may want to see, those caused by a busy run, are still reported by the scheduler.

area: agent files: missing method key line
old: 784f78d: a key missing from a map that is the value of another key was reported at the line of the map's first key (the value line), one line below the parent key.
new: A key missing from a map that is the value of another key is reported at the parent key's line, where the user adds the missing key. Only the line moves; the path and code are the same.
why: Missing key reported at the parent key line, old app used the value line. The parity fixtures already expect the key line. Decided in HAL-2045 (decisions/maya/HAL-2045-yaml-missing-key-parent.md), approved by Liam (CTO) on HAL-2122; not for HAL-58.

old: 784f78d read three old layouts and noted each with an info message that pointed to `studio migrate`: a projects/ folder for hubs, a flows/ folder in a hub, and org.yaml for workspace.yaml.
new: Files are read only from the places the file kinds declare, so files in those old layouts are listed as ignored and give no message. Without workspace.yaml, the workspace gets the old loader's own error "Missing workspace.yaml".
why: One place per kind keeps the loader free of special cases, and a new kind is read without a change to it (HAL-1522). The board decided on HAL-2299 (9 Nov) that old layouts stay quietly ignored: no note and no migrate step, and any help moving off them would be a new ask for the board.

old.message: Hubs used to be called projects: run `studio migrate` to move projects/ to hubs/
Legacy flows/ folder: run `studio migrate` to move it to workflows/
org.yaml is now called workspace.yaml; run studio migrate to rename it

area: workspace loader: a routine's cron and time zone
old: A bad cron field gave the bare problem, such as Routine "month-end": "61" is outside 0-59, and an unknown zone Routine "month-end": Unknown time zone "Mars/Olympus", without a full stop.
new: The routines package's own messages: a bad field is named, as in Minute: "61" is outside 0-59., and each message ends with a full stop (routines.check-time-zone for the zone).
why: The routines package already words these messages this way, and the loader passes them on rather than keep a second wording. Naming the field tells a person which of the five values to fix.

area: connector files: tools.approve of the wrong type
old: 784f78d packages/core/schema/src/index.ts: tools.approve was only a list of tool names, so a value of another type failed with invalid_type at tools.approve.
new: tools.approve is a list of tool names or the word all, so a value that is neither fails with invalid_union at tools.approve, on the same line. The file still fails.
why: A new MCP connector starts with approve: all, so every tool asks a person first (launch claim C89, HAL-1219; the format change was agreed on HAL-1257). Only the problem code changes; the file fails at the same place.

area: parallel state: order of sibling branches
old: 784f78d's runner started a parallel state's branches, logged their agent.started and agent.finished events, and wrote their context.updated results and the output map in the order the file lists them (the base fixture's invoice: vendor, then amount).
new: The engine does all of these in name order (amount, then vendor). Only the order of sibling branch entries inside one parallel state differs: the set of branches, each branch's own events, every result and the final output are the same.
why: Runs keep their definitions as canonical JSON (HAL-186 decision 5), which sorts keys, so the file's order is gone when a run reads them. Each branch writes only under its own name, so the order changes the log, not a result. Decided by Liam on HAL-3703; if a fixture shows a result that depends on branch order, this entry no longer applies and the question goes back to him.

old: 784f78d gave every run of a test the next ID from one counter: the test run test_1, its child runs test_2, test_3 and so on, in the order they started.
new: The engine names a child run after its parent and the step that started it: <parent>.<seq of the step>, and <parent>.<seq>.<item> for a foreach item (test_1.23, test_1.2.0). The compare names both sides run_1, run_2, ... in the order the runs started.
why: A child run ID made from the parent log is the same each time the parent decision is replayed, so a start asked for twice finds the run it already started instead of starting a second one. A counter would give a new ID on every replay.

old: 784f78d wrote a short hash of the old definitions, sha256:<16 hex>, in run.started and the summary.
new: definitionsVersion is the full SHA-256 of the definitions kept for the run, which is the hash of their blob. The compare leaves it out on both sides.
why: The run reads its definitions back from the blob store by this hash (HAL-186 decision 5), so it has to be the blob hash. The definitions themselves differ in shape, so the two hashes can never match.

old: 784f78d wrote run.waiting with the state, the events it takes and its timers.
new: run.waiting also carries the answer labels and the wait step description (labels, title). The compare leaves them out of the new events.
why: Every place that shows a waiting run reads the same words from the log (HAL-1290 inbox, halonic runs). They are added fields: the old ones are unchanged.

old: 784f78d wrote workflow.finished with the child run ID and status only.
new: For a foreach item that runs a workflow, workflow.finished also carries the child final context. The compare leaves it out of the new events.
why: A foreach keeps each item result in its own log, so a run read on its own shows every item result without reading the child logs. It is an added field.

old: 784f78d summary had one approval (or null) and no fields for subscriptions, failure reasons, waiting text, answers a run could not try, or the last event.
new: The summary has an approvals list and adds subscriptionCalls, reason, answerLabels, waitingFor, lastWaitingAt, cantTry, lastSeq and updatedAt. The compare leaves the old approval and the new fields out; every other field is compared.
why: Approvals routed by callId need a list (E5, HAL-1257); the other fields come from their own requirements in core/events. None changes a field the old summary had.

old: With concurrency: 2, 784f78d ran the items in batches of two: items 0 and 1, then item 2 once both had finished.
new: The engine starts the next item as soon as one finishes, so at most two wait at once. Only the order of item events in one foreach state differs. The compare sorts each stretch of item events by item on both sides.
why: concurrency is a limit on items running at once, as engine.foreach-state says. A batch leaves a slot unused while the slower item of the batch runs.

old: 784f78d's studio test printed one line per test as <hub>/<workflow>: <name> and "N passed"; studio run printed every event of the log as a numbered line and "Run <id>: <status>"; errors were the bare message, such as Unknown workflow "nope" in hub "billing".
new: halonic test and halonic run print the sentences of the CLI's message catalogue: a heading, one line per test or step, a summary and a next step, and errors as a problem and its fix. The compare leaves stdout and stderr out on both sides; the exit code and every stored run are still compared.
why: Every sentence the user reads comes from the catalogue by key (cli-output, approved by the board on HAL-2123), so none of the old words is kept. The catalogue's own tests check the words.

old: 784f78d's CLI exited with 1 for every failure: a failed run, a filter that kept no test, an event the state doesn't take, an unknown workflow, input that isn't JSON and a missing argument.
new: halonic exits with 1 only for a failed run or test, 2 for a wrong command line or input (an event the wait doesn't take, input that isn't JSON, no workflow, a filter that keeps no test) and 4 for something not found (an unknown workflow). The compare turns the new 2 and 4 to 9 into 1; 3, for a workspace that isn't trusted, is never turned.
why: A script can tell its own mistake from a failed run and from a missing workflow (HAL-1994, decided on HAL-1984). The base is trusted in the compare, so a 3 there is a real difference.

area: CLI calls: runs of studio test
old: 784f78d's studio test stored every run of every test in the workspace, as .studio/runs/test_<n>.jsonl (15 runs for the base's 8 tests).
new: halonic test runs the tests on empty in-memory stores and writes nothing. The compare leaves the old test calls' runs out; the runs themselves are compared test by test in the run-log compare (test-runner.parity-run-logs).
why: A test shouldn't change the workspace or the person's run list, and must never need trust: it runs on the test model with nothing sent anywhere (cli-output 3.3).

old: 784f78d wrote run.failed with the state and the error only.
new: run.failed also carries a reason, such as error or budget. The compare leaves it out of the new events.
why: Studio and the CLI pick the failed run's words and fix by the reason, not by parsing the error text. It is an added, optional field: logs without it read as before.

area: CLI calls: an agent's answer that isn't JSON
old: 784f78d failed the run with Agent "checker" did not reply with valid JSON.
new: The error quotes the answer and says what to do: Agent "checker" answered "paper", which isn't the JSON its output asks for. Tighten the agent's instructions or use a larger model. The compare gives both one plain form; that the run failed, where and for which agent is still compared.
why: The person sees what the agent answered and how to fix it, without opening the log (HAL-4756).

area: CLI calls: a foreach item whose child run failed
old: 784f78d failed the run with Item 1 of 1: Workflow "line-check" failed: <error>, counting items from 1.
new: The error is Workflow "line-check" failed in item 0 of for-each state "each": <error>, counting items from 0 as item does in the events. The compare gives both one plain form; the item, the workflow and the error after it are still compared.
why: Every failure of an item's child run is wrapped the same way, a budget stop too, and the item's number matches the item field of its events.

why: The product calls this setting the assistant model; "session AI" was retired in the microcopy (section 1.2). Naming assistant.model tells a person which key to fix, and models.yaml where the aliases live.
